utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you, but our defendant insists, insists on informing this Trial Chamber of his objections and his comments relating to how things are -- how people are brought before this Tribunal because he is claiming that the handcuffs that they usually put on his hands are too tight, and they leave marks on his arms and hands. I promised to him that I would look into this, but my client insisted that I bring this up before this Trial Chamber. He also wanted me to bring up that for the third day in a row now, he has not had his glasses because he -- the prison -- detention unit administration took upon itself to repair his glasses, and so he has not had his own glasses for several days now and has had to use borrowed glasses, and so he wanted me to bring this up before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I must say, the Trial Chamber would be very sympathetic to anybody who had to be here with somebody else's glasses. I don't know what the need was for the repair, but does he have his own glasses now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. His glasses were sent for repair before this hearing began, and he used -- my client used the glasses he borrowed from somebody else who did not have a hearing last week, but this person, whose glasses my client is using now, does have a hearing this week so needs the glasses himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How long ago were the glasses sent for repair?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On January 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. The Trial Chamber, of course, has no jurisdiction to make any orders in respect of this, but I'll have the registry make an inquiry about the glasses, and we'll draw your client's complaint to the attention of the prison authorities. If you do have to follow up anything about that, you should make a complaint to the, first of all, the registrar, and if he is unable to resolve it, to the president. But one hopes that if the complaint is made now and officially to the prison authorities, they will get on and do something about it. If there is any further problem, I suggest you approach the registrar first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And I apologise for taking up the time to bring this up, but my client wanted this to -- wanted me to inform the Trial Chamber of this, and I had to respect his wishes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You need not apologise. It is a matter which we would be concerned about whether we had authority to do something about it or not. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday when we were talking about the list of employees, you took out a piece of paper in front of you to check some dates. What was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a paper document from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have it with you now?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date does this document have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a date when the International Red Cross entered KP Dom for the first time, 23rd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please show this -- would you please tell us the date of the document, when this document was made? I would like to know what document it is.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Document was issued on the 24th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document should be in the trial binder, and it is -- has the identification number 259, but I got the impression yesterday that the Defence wants to see the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, Witness, could you please, with the help of the usher, show around the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I have a look? Your Honours, this is indeed the document 259, the original of this document ID 259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, show it to Mr. Bakrac. If he wants to check it against the copy before the copy is tendered, he may see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So you have no objection, then, to the tender of the copy, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The copy of the document ID 259 will be Exhibit P259, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just if you look at the document it says, on the document it says the ICRC was notified -- you were notified as present on the 30th of August, 1992. Did the Red Cross visit the KP Dom on that date, and were you registered in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was registered in Sarajevo with the Red Cross there as a person who disappeared in Foca, and it wasn't until 1993 when that International Red Cross entered the KP Dom because they were not allowed to enter it prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it come that you were registered in Sarajevo with the Red Cross as a missing person? Who actually -- how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My relatives registered me in Sarajevo. They found out that I had disappeared, and they immediately informed the Red Cross in Sarajevo about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the document there is also the line, "Was registered by ICRC delegate on the 23rd of June, 1993." Is that correct? Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is when they entered for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says also the release date here on this document as the 6th of October, 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also receive a document from the State Commission of the Location of Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, from the State Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from Mr. Masovic, and the date was 10th of May, 1992, until the 6th of October, 1992. The place of exchange is indicated here, and that is the bridge called bridge Bratsvo-Jedinstvo in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is document ID 258. And as I see, the witness has the original with him as well. Would the Defence want to check the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you any objection to the tender of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Exhibit - I'm sorry - the document ID 258 will be Exhibit P258 and it will again be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With the help of the usher, I would like to have P3 put to the witness. That's the list of employees of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, it is not necessary that we talk about all of the employees listed on this lengthy list. I will talk -- I will always refer to the number this person has on this list, and we only talk about some specific persons. First of all, would you please look --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the translation is document P3A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First look at number 3, Milorad Krnojelac. You have already told us when you saw him and how long he was in the KP Dom. In the last row -- the last column, there is a remark on this list referring to his position as acting warden from the 18th of April till the 17th of July. Do you remember the 17th of July? Did anything change in the KP Dom at that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Sekulovic, Ranko, replaced - I apologise - Sekulovic, Zoran, replaced Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 17th of July, 1992, does that stick in -- and did anything happen on this day? Do you recall anything particular?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go further on in the list to the person number 6, Dragisa Milic. Was this person working in the prison when you were detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a truck driver at the farm, and before the war he worked as a psychologist at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he work as a psychologist during your detention?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He worked as a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now please move on to the person number 9, Risto Ivanovic. And was he -- what was he doing while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivanovic, Risto, also known as Rile, we had a guard with that name and he was there the entire time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he treat the detainees? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well. Because everybody praised him. He was fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And now move on to number 17, Dragomir Blagojevic. Was he in the prison, and what was he doing during -- we are talking during your time of detention only.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagojevic, Dragomir was a guard at the KP Dom before the war and he was there during the war as a guard. Muslims' complaint of him that he was mistreating them and provoking them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you look at the dates when he was -- you see the column number 4 with the date when he started to work, and the column number 5 when he stopped working, and there is a gap in there from 10 September 1992 to 2 September 1993. My question is: Was he there in the KP Dom all the time during your detention or was there actually a one-year gap?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated yesterday that they used to go to the front line, but I did see him at the KP Dom when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the person number 20, and go through from 20 to 26. Were these people in the KP Dom, and what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perisic, Vasilije came in later. Kunarac, Slavko worked at the farm. He was killed in Ustikolina when he stepped on a mine. Stefanovic, Predrag was there, worked the entire time; Milic, Milivoje as well. Miro Sekulovic came in later. Zdravko Ivanovic worked at the farm. Milenko Cancar came in later. Milan Bogdanic worked there the entire time. Momcilo Popadic worked in security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just mentioned them. How did they treat the detainees? Is there anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to single out Predrag Stefanovic, Milivoje Milic, and I would simply like to highlight these two as those who behaved inappropriately towards the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "behaved inappropriately," what did they do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard from the inmates that they were beaten by them at gate 1 and in that Passing Room. I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please move on to the person number 30. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Risto Gojanovic worked in security. He was a tutor, educator at the KP Dom, and he also worked at the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean he was not a guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a guard. He was in security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And how did he treat the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard anything bad as far as he's concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person number 32, Slavko Koroman, what can you tell us about him and his position?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Koroman was the guard supervisor before the war. He retired also before the war, and since they didn't have -- since they were short-staffed, they used to hire or call back the retired individuals as well. Slavko Koroman was before the war some kind of a supervisor, but he didn't stay there for a long time. Perhaps a month to a month and a half. I haven't heard anything bad about him, either. And as far as the rest are concerned, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the persons under the number 34 to 36, what can you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elcic mistreated Muslims, that's what I heard, Pljevaljcic as well, and I haven't heard anything bad about Zoran Lalovic. Risto Matovic was a driver. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And person 41, Momcilo Ristanovic, what did he do? What can you tell us about his behaviour?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as am concerned, he was fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now --

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the persons 45 to -- through to actually 52.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milovan Vukovic worked in security. I heard that he mistreated people as well. Obrenovic, Radomir, I heard bad things about him. Matovic, Mladen -- Matovic, Zoran, he's the one who locked me up in the solitary confinement cell. Ljubomir Petkovic worked in security. I didn't hear anything bad about him. Milan Perisic, he got sick and I didn't really see him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 51, Miro Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miro Prodanovic, I also heard bad things of him. He was a supervisor throughout the war. He never left the KP Dom during that time. Vukovic, Radovan, I also heard bad things about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "bad things," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mistreated and beat people. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have also talked about Mr. Rasevic. Could you please go to number 55 who was the -- 55 and 56.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savic, Jovo, was also a guard. I heard very bad things of him. Milenko Burilo, this is a person that I heard the worst things about. He was one of those who beat people the most. Everybody knew him, and his nickname was Busi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the persons listed under 65 and 66.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladicic, Milenko, I heard that he beat people. I heard bad things about him. He works at the KP Dom now; he is there still to this date. And what was the next number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sixty-six.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milivoje Milutinovic, I also heard bad things about him. He is from Miljevina. He was a guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 70?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Mijovic. He worked in security, but he was there for a very short time, and I didn't see a lot of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we have already talked about Mr. Radojica Tesevic under number 72, and it says here on this document that he was the appointed director of the farm unit in August 1993. Are you aware -- did you see him in the prison during your detention time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. He toured the furniture factory in 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person 79, Rade Gagovic, who he was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a rehabilitation officer in KP Dom. I would see him in a military uniform, but not often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person 91?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Pejic. He was at the KP Dom as well, in security. I heard bad things about him as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now these people listed under -- beginning in 94, from 94 through to 113, what kind of staff was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Misko Markovic, Vide Boskovic, Zoran Novovic, Dojcilo Davidovic, Slobodan Micevic, Nebojsa Krunic, Radivoje Jegdic, Petar Gagovic, Milomir Malic, guard, Zdravka Matovic, Rosa Babic, Savka Pavlovic, Gojko Dragicevic, Mira Pavlovic, Jovanka Krunic, Desa Ikonic, Ljiljana Radovic, Zorka Ivnovic. Branko Stefanovic, I don't know him. Jelisavka Djokic, she didn't work there. Well, this is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but where did these people -- except for Maric, Maric, the guard, where did these other people work? Were they actually in the KP Dom? Did you see them there and ...

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these ladies at KP Dom. Jegdic, Radivoje, I saw occasionally. Krunic, Nebojsa, occasionally. Slobodan Mircevic, occasionally. They worked in security, either within the compound or the -- or on the outside. They had some kind of a bunker near the cinema, and they also had a path that they guarded, that those who worked in Maglic outside of the KP Dom guarded. And they would use contacts, there were special contacts to be assigned to work at the KP Dom, rather than go and work at the factory, rather than go to the front. And these ladies that are mentioned here, some of them worked at the prison quarters and some of them worked in administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these people listed here, did they actually have contact with the detainees, and how did they then treat the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have any contact with them because they were just too far so that they communicated very, very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person listed under 116, yesterday you mentioned that he was a judge before the war, but he did not work as a judge at that time, or was he related to this court-martial that you mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is a matter that has been investigated by the Prosecutor when he appeared before -- before he appeared as counsel here. What is the purpose of all of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Only I want -- the Prosecution wants to point out that there was no court-martial in the prison as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him? Why are we going through all of this? Is this for some future investigation, or is it relevant to this present case?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it is relevant to this case. That is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. May I suggest, if that's all you're interested in, why don't you just ask the witness. But Mr. Prodanovic has been appearing before this Trial Chamber, actually, as counsel; and at the time when he first appeared, the Prosecutor raised this issue that he had worked as a guard in a prison, and it was fully investigated, and it was then stated that there was nothing known against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I know, Your Honour. But the witness yesterday said that Mr. Prodanovic was a judge, and he did not then tell us what he was actually doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He said he was a judge before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Which he may or may not have been. He was a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I'm not sure why we're spending all this time on this very long document going through each one, one by one by one. What is the point of it all?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The point is that we want to have the guards pointed out and certain people that were mentioned by witnesses, what position they had and how they treated the detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if that's what you're doing, most of these haven't been mentioned in any of the evidence so far. But let's get on with it. If it's going to be something that can be dealt with speedily, just lead him to the ones which are really relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person number 120, the person number 120, what can you tell us about him, 120 on the list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaso Pljevaljcic was there throughout. He was also a supervisor or rather, a guard. Bad things were said about him, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person 135, Vitomir Micevic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another guard, and bad things were said about him too, about how he treated people and behaved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person number 137?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radomir Papovic, he was wounded in the early days of the war, did not come for work, but he did turn up later. Well, and he was -- well, here and there, as far as I'm concerned. He was quite decent. But some may have complained of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last person, 143.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Svetislav Krunic also came later. I heard no complaints against him. And he is still employed by the KP Dom. He's their senior guard, supervisor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough with the list. Witness, did you suffer any physical or mental consequences as a result of the conditions at the KP Dom, you personally?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, I did. Naturally, I did suffer some psychological consequences. I had to undergo surgery when I arrived in Sarajevo, and abdominal intervention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this surgery relate to your detention, the conditions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have, because I had no complaints before the war, as I went for regular medical check-ups every year and I was quite fit to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, these are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours. I'm looking for a paper. Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, sir. I'm Mihajlo Bakrac and I'm one of the counsel defending the accused Milorad Krnojelac. In the beginning of your testimony here you explained where your house was and what had happened to it. Do you know and can you tell us where was Milorad Krnojelac's house? Do you know that and did you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac's house was in Donje Polje neighbourhood community, and that is where I lived too. It is about two kilometres away from my house, nearer the elementary school Ivan Goran Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what happened to the house of the accused Krnojelac in the early days of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware if there were any other houses in the neighbourhood, I mean Serb houses, set on fire?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Across the Ivan Goran Kovacic elementary school there were other houses torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke about the capacity of the KP Dom before the war, that is, (redacted). And if I understood what you said, you said that the KP Dom could accommodate between 1.000 and 1.200 prisoners but it also included outside buildings. And after that you also mentioned the farm for about 100 prisoners and the fish farm for some 20, 25 men. So could we then agree that the capacity of the inner compound of the prison was somewhere between 1.000 and 1.100 men?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted), I found in the prison itself about 1.020, 1.030 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the inner compound, which does not include any outside building or outposts?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's buildings 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that the women's prison at Velecevo was under the supervision of the male prison. By this, did you mean the time before the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the armed conflict. And Velecevo later on was turned into military headquarters, and now it is the faculty of theology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. (redacted) (redacted), prisoners were taken to work and that they were remunerated accordingly. Does that mean that they were all paid the same amounts of money as free people, that is, as professionals?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the construction business, for instance, those who worked at various construction sites in Sarajevo, and what they received in salary was even more than I got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was that an exception or a rule? Did all the prisoners earn that much?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was an exception.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you also said a great deal about the organisational layout of the KP Dom before the war, before the general mobilisation, and what you said yesterday about the structure and layout of the KP Dom, that you told us yesterday, did you tell us about it in peacetime conditions or later on, in wartime, when you were there as a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime. But again, it was the same structure; the same organisation continued in time of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke yesterday about disciplinary sanctions. My question is: (redacted), was it possible that in case of some excesses by a convict, the guard himself would take that person to the isolation cell, that is, himself sanctions the convict?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard had no authority to pronounce any punishment. All he could do was lock a person up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about that, but I think it remained rather vague. When you arrived in the -- or rather, when you were detained in the KP Dom, did you find there a certain number of persons of Serb ethnicity who had been serving there the final judgements?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find any one of them; Serbs, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke how there were some Serbs detained in the KP Dom but in a separate part of building B.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detention of Serbs began when they refused to go to the front or because of fighting at the front, because of a murder, because of murders in Trebinje, Gacko and Bileca. That is, the court had finally begun to function and they therefore started to bring them to the Foca penitentiary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware if there were some Serbs working at the farm, I mean those who had been sentenced and were serving their sentence there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that, but I know that two Muslims from the penitentiary went up there and worked at the farm, and that a woman from Stolac was a woman who took their meals and looked after those men working at the farm, and that woman was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you had seen the accused at the Sutjeska stadium, at a rally. Could you tell us exactly where was the stage in which all these speakers stood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I know they were among the audience -- I remember they were among the audience, but I think that it was in the centre, but I'm not quite sure. Quite close to the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "public," yesterday you spoke about stalls, about stands. Were those the only ones that were at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were there and the public were there in -- on those stands, in those stalls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that that is where you saw the accused?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was with all the other front men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were also a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I attended rallies of all the parties, because I was not a member of any party and I was simply curious to know. Anyone could attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a pleasure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned an incident involving Balic. Is it true that you gave two statements to OTP investigators and one to the Security Centre in Sarajevo and that you did not mention the incident with Balic in any one of those statements?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. That was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, when you are answering one of Mr. Bakrac's questions, you should understand that the interpreter has to interpret both the question and the answer, so would you please pause before you answer to enable the interpreter to catch up. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question was: Why didn't you mention the incident with Balic before and that it came up only yesterday while you were answering the Prosecutor's questions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose I did not remember it at the time, because so many things happened, and one can't remember it all, two and a half years in a camp. One really had to make an effort to remember it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday my learned friend asked you, but we did not get an answer, so I'm taking it up again. When was Aziz Torlak taken for exchange? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall the date, but I know that it was around half past 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning one July, August, September morning, and I heard from a Serb that the exchange had failed and that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You say July, August, September. Which year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was it 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned an incident with Salko Mandzo. Where did you see him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Salko Mandzo, called Kelta, worked at a farm for a while, and he was in my room and he told me about the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that in the KP Dom surgery?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. He was not in the surgery. He was in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified how you went to see the doctor "in our surgery, in our clinic." Whom did you find there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that medical technician, Mandzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was being administered medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. Which Mandzo was being extended aid?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Kelta, but the medical technician Mandzo, and I mentioned his name yesterday. It escapes me now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who was extending aid to him in your clinic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I got that when you said "in our surgery, in our clinic," I understood that it was in the prison. But who was it who was extending aid to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Jokanovic, a nurse, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the KP Dom on a daily basic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from him, were there any physicians there, for instance, Dr. Dobrilovic, Vladicic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days of the war I used to see Vladicic, and while there were any medicines, they came. And while there were any other medical supplies, before it was all removed from there and taken away, they came; but after all that, only -- Gojko was the only one who worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that guards would call out and take away prisoners to gate 1 of the KP Dom. Do you know who took them over from them there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards called them out, took to the gate, but nobody could see who was -- who would take them over from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 17th of October in 1994, did you make a statement to the Public Security Centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it jog your memory if I showed you the signature on the statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might very well be that I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in that statement you said as of June -- in June 1992, beating and harassment of prisoners at night began. This was done by members of the military police who would arrive to the -- who would arrive in the KP Dom at sunset?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards took them out and who tortured people, that I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, is it true that you stated this to the Public Security Centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it says so, then perhaps I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct to say that you made two statements to OTP investigators on the 25th and 26th of June, 1996, the first one, and the second on the 22nd of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I gave one statement to the Tribunal in Marsal, which is the former JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not give them two statements, the first one on the 25th, 26th of June, 1996, when the interview was conducted by Racine Manas and the interpreter was Amira Bojadzija; and the second one when my learned friend, who also conducted examination-in-chief, and Investigator Thapa with interpreter Kanita Halilovic took the statement from you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I only gave one statement, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it, in 1996 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1998. Before that you did not make -- give any statements to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I can remember, but I may have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall read to you the beginning of the second statement, the one of 1998: "I have given a previous statement to the ICTY." Is that true or is it not true, what I have just read to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in one of those statements say that prisoners would always be taken out between 1800 and 1900 hours?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around half past three?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Between 1800 and 1900, prisoners would always be taken between 1800 and 1900?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, I did. That is, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you said yesterday, that they were taken out between 1500 and 1700, was not correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken out between half past three until 1900 because it was summertime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said that it was correct that they were taken out between 1800 and 1900, between 6.00 and 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, he hasn't said that. He has agreed that that's what he said in the statement. You are asking him, "Didn't you say in the statement," and he said "that is correct." Now, if you want to say that what he said in the statement is correct, you'd better get him to confirm it. But whilst I have interrupted you, may I point out that the witness has not accepted the statements that you have put to him, from the statement he gave to the Sarajevo Security Centre. He just said he may have said them. He has not accepted that he made a statement in 1996 to the tribunal's investigators or to the OTP's investigators. So you should not assume that you can rely upon anything he says in those statements at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took it, Your Honours, that he said, "Oh, yes, that's what I said," and then there was a full stop, and then after that he said, "That is correct." I took it that he confirmed that it was correct with respect to the time, and this is the reason why I asked this question. But I think that now after this entire discussion it would be useless to ask this question again, so I will get on with my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't want to divert you, but I want to warn you that this is not the situation, for example, that we debated several times last year where there had been a complete acceptance of what had been said in the statement. You have not got, in my view, an acceptance of anything other than that he had said in the statement that they were always taken out between 1800 and 1900, where he went on to say -- reassert what he said yesterday was the correct view. But I don't want you to pass on, on any assumption that you've got an acceptance from the witness. It's a matter for you what you want to do about it. I don't want to divert you from your task, but I want to make it very clear that you have not got, in my view, a clear acceptance of anything other than that one statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Let's leave it at this because since the witness has already heard what we had just discussed, I think that that would certainly influence his answers, so this is why I will start with my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you discussed the so-called passing room or through room. Did I understand you correctly that the window of this passing room faced the street in front of the entrance into the KP Dom and also in front of the bridge across the Drina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the window faced the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this passing room have a window facing the inner circle of the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that between this passing room and the inner compound there was a hallway, and then after the hallway came the second row of rooms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in one of your statements you stated that Savo Todovic was in charge of prisoners and forced labour?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also state that Savo Todovic was in prison day and night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a bed in his office, but I didn't normally see him in the evenings. I remember that once he took me out around 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in one of your statements you stated the following, and this is a statement given to the Prosecution on 25th and 26th of June, page 3 in the B/C/S version, fifth paragraph: "In KP Dom I was treated fairly, except for the fact that I was forced to work mostly in the agricultural area. I knew the guards well, and every time when I complained about certain assignments given to me, they wouldn't do anything to me."

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated yesterday that they treated you strictly officially and were even worse than that, rougher sometimes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was even locked up in the solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever, before or just ever, notice that Milorad Krnojelac had some anti-Muslim sentiments?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in your statements given to the Prosecution and the Public Security Centre, you stated that you believed that nobody ever saw Milorad Krnojelac present at the time when the prisoners or detainees were taken out for beatings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also in your statements state that Todovic and Rasevic would come in to check on the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also state it that you never saw Krnojelac do that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also state to the OTP investigators very clearly, obviously to a very clear question put to you, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I began, Your Honour, but I don't know if you this individual whose name that I was about to mention is a protected witness. I'm referring to a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean this person is a witness in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is scheduled to come in to testify as a Trial Chamber's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know that we have ever asked for any witness to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have him on the list, but my colleague here is aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is the witness that is summoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We have given him --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have given him a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: However, yesterday we used the name because no protective measures are requested yet, but it may, of course, happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That doesn't help by saying that. I think that better be redacted what you just said. I don't remember, (redacted) (redacted); do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: RJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So you can refer to him as RJ, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours, but I don't know if we should for a moment switch into private session so that I can say this to the witness, or should I simply put it in writing, this witness's name, and then refer to this witness (redacted)? Whatever you think, whatever you think is easiest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As long as the witness knows who you are speaking to. Have you got the document you could show him? That would be the quickest way of dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the witness is nodding, so that means he probably knows who I'm referring to, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you clearly state to the OTP investigators the following: "RJ did not mention to me that Krnojelac had found a corpse in his office."

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never stated this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not state what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything pertaining to this corpse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a completely new statement for you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to avoid any confusion, I'm repeating here that when clearly asked, explicitly asked by the Prosecution, you replied that he did not tell you that Krnojelac had found a corpse. So I take it that this is then correct, based on what you had just told us.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness never mentioned any corpse or was aware of any kind of corpse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in your statement to the Prosecution - or rather, I apologise - in your statement to the Public Security Centre in Sarajevo, you stated that you were admitted to KP Dom by Pljevaljcic, Vlatko; and Rasevic, Cedo; and that the military police searched you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated yesterday that the military arrested me, that Mitar Rasevic was present, and Pljevaljcic, Vlatko. They were present at the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is very short, so I will read it to you: "I was admitted to the KP Dom by Pljevaljcic, Vlatko; and Rasevic, Cedo; and the search was conducted by the military police. Mitar Rasevic sent me to Room 18." Is it true what I have just read to you? Did you actually state this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part is not correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar Rasevic personally brought me into KP Dom. Vlatko Pljevaljcic was at the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who conducted the search? Who searched you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody searched me, because all of my former colleagues were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is not true that you said this in your statement to the Public Security Centre in Sarajevo. Did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave an oral statement and I have no idea what they wrote down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be so kind and tell us: Do you know who is a person called Boro Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Ivanovic was an educator and teacher in a commune Godjeno, which is located 12 kilometres away from Foca. I heard from the Muslims, who were involved in forced labour, that he was the security commander, but I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was the security commander for the town of Foca; right? You mentioned this individual in your statement given to the Public Security Centre in Sarajevo and also in your statement given to the Prosecution. In your statement given to the Prosecution, at page 3, in your first statement of June 25th and 26th, you said, verbatim: "Boro Ivanovic, who was the commander of the security police in the prison complex, I saw once, but he did not enter the detention facilities." So here you stated that he was the commander of the security police in the prison quarters.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how could I have stated that when this is not -- when this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was not his position? I know who was in charge of the security police in the prison complex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I just read out to you is not correct; you in fact did not state this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I am stating now is correct, and this is that Boro Ivanovic was the security commander for the town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the military structure?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the military structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us: Do you know how many Muslim detainees remained in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I simply know how many were there in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us how many were there in 1994?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty-eight. Seventy-eight people, approximately, came for an exchange at Kula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all -- were all of those exchanged from the KP Dom in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No Muslims remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of those 78, were some people from other camps or other prisons or perhaps from Kula?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kula we found about 20 people from the KP Dom in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So 50 or 58 people could have been from the KP Dom in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a figure of 68.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I have just two more questions and then I would ask you to take a look at a photograph. Yesterday you discussed a vehicle, Zastava make, known as Kedi, and you said that this vehicle was used to transport fish. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that during the time when you were detained in KP Foca, do you know whether the economic units of the KP Dom were functioning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A farm, economic unit Drina, and a mine were functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the fishery was transferred from Jeleca to Bukovice at the time when you were detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the fish hatchery completely left the location of Jeleca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that some of that fish that was transferred to Bukovice was also transported into stores?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't wander about the city, so I could not have seen that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me: Do you know whether fish, like people, have blood in their bodies?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not say no. He said yes, they do have blood; fish have blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know - and this is something that we verified in our document - on June 23rd, 1993, when the International Red Cross came in, do you know whether Milorad Krnojelac was still the warden of the KP Dom at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Sekulovic came in August or September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you will certainly agree with me that in June, Milorad Krnojelac was still the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And please tell me also whether in May or some other month of 1992 a delegation from the International Red Cross also visited the KP Dom. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would ask the usher to put this photograph, 7442, in front of the witness - this is the top photograph - and to enlarge this segment here so that we can see the building above the administration building. I would ask you to please zoom in on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Which part do you want -- to the left or to the right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to the right of the tree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This, of course is a photograph that was taken from a higher position than the street. I don't know if you realise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I realise that, Your Honours, but I want to ask this witness to answer something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think - and I think that you will be able to do that now - can you please count how many windows are there from the tree until the end of the building, and I have in mind the prison complex.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eight. Thank you. Can you please tell me, if you can see this from the photograph: Between the administrative building and cinema -- or rather, where is the border between the administrative building and cinema? Near which window?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please count from the right side and look at where is the division between the cinema and the administrative building. From the right end of the building, how many windows are until that line separating those two buildings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, I would like the witness to be shown photograph number 7529, the bottom photograph, and once again I would like the same -- I would like the technician to zoom in on the same detail. Your Honours, this is a photograph that was taken from the level of the road, on the other side of the river with respect to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how many windows do you see now from the tree to the right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking from the cinema, is the cinema obstructing the remaining number of windows?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only half of the window can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see all of the eight windows that you were able to see before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only half of the windows can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean half of eight, which means four windows?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So three and a half. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need this photograph anymore. Thank you. I would simply like to verify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Bakrac. It's not clear as to whether the photographs were taken on the same angle, so that you would have to be able to produce some evidence that they are before you started to say there were five windows that were hidden. From my recollection -- I was only watching them on the screen, but they were taken from slightly different angles as well, not only from different elevations, but from different angles, which may affect your next submission at some stage that there were five windows hidden behind the cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot establish now what was the difference in an angle. I simply wanted us to establish this, and I did promise you that we will make photographs from the Room 23. But what I needed now was to establish the facts that we have based on the evidence presented by the Prosecution. It is up to you to evaluate whether we succeeded to prove what we are trying to suggest here, but perhaps this angle could have been a bit different, at least could have shown a picture different by about half of a window, but I simply wanted to once again establish what is visible based on the photographs presented by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm not trying to challenge what you're doing at all; I'm trying to assist you by saying that if you want to ask us to do a mathematical exercise to say how many windows have been hidden by the cinema there, it may not be quite as easy as it appears at the moment, so that you will be able to apply your mind to what does have to be shown so that we can then work out which are the three windows or three and a half windows that are shown in that last photograph. I am not concerned one way or the other about this issue; I'm only trying to point out to you that I think you should apply your mind to how you go about proving it if you want us to make some assumptions or some conclusions about the number of windows or which rooms those windows are that you can see in that last photograph. And I'm drawing it to your attention now so that it will be in your mind, I hope, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will keep this in mind, but I needed the witness to state -- to reassert this, and this will be my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you properly that Room 23 had two windows in the dormitory section and two windows in the living-room section?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that those were four windows from the right side, right end of the building number 2, the last four windows of the right end of the building 2? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, this could perhaps be a good time to have a break. I have only a few questions remaining to put to the witness and they pertain to the rooms, and then I would end my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any way of taking the witness who is coming next, who has voice distortion, through the exercise of having the microphone adjusted to him so we don't have to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that can be done during the adjournment. We'll resume, then, at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the detention unit has provided a response to the complaints, and I'll give you a copy of the e-mail, and there would be one for the Prosecution as well. I think you'll find that it will probably be sorted out reasonably well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. This was really an unexpected efficiency, and I hope the accused will be happy. This was really a very prompt solution to his problem. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you like to continue cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I promised that I would be brief, and I have one more question and one list with some names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us yesterday that from Room 23 you could see some of the Drina. Are you saying that you could see the segment of the Drina opposite your room, that is, the far away part of the bridge opposite the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Room 23 one can see half of the bridge, that is, the farther side of the bridge, and perhaps a little less of one half of the river, again, from the farther side of the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was, could you from Room 23 see part of the River Drina below the bridge and around the bridge?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not below the bridge, not under the bridge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall now read out some names to you slowly and will invite you to tell me if you can remember where were those persons when you mentioned them and told us that they were taken away. Which room was Salem Bico in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In building 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either 14 or 15, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Abdurahman Cankusic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Juso Dzamalija?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Juso Dzamalija, 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kemal Dzelilovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ramo Dzendusic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixteen, building 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Halim Konjo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was in either 15 or 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Fuad Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which room he was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Krunoslav Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was in building 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hamid Ramovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Building 2, and I believe it was 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Husein Rikalo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mithat Rikalo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all three of them were in building 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know the room, and were all three of them in one and the same room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all in building 1, but whether they were all in one and the same room, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kemal Tulek?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemal Tulek was in the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before the isolation cell, do you know where he was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was brought from Bileca and directly put into the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the isolation cell he was taken out of the KP Dom, you said?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Enes Uzunovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while he was in building 1, that is 11, and then he was transferred to 18 in building 2, and then he was taken through gate 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Room 18, you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Munib Veiz?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-three. No, no, no, excuse me, excuse me. Fifteen, it was building 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same thing, Room 15, building 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your evidence is now finished. Thank you for giving evidence to the Tribunal. You are free to leave. You should, however, wait a moment while the blinds are being lowered so that you will not be seen by members of the public.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, meanwhile the witness -- the technical things are replaced, I have one small technical matter, and that is, when we entered into evidence the document P258, it was overseen that there was also a translation to it, and that is the translation 258A, and we did not -- we forgot to enter this into evidence. This is simply the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then that document will become Exhibit P258A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The document with the witness' name and some other pseudonyms to which he may be referring will be Exhibit P416, and it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, will you please make the solemn declaration in the document which is now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has granted you protection measures in this case in relation to your name, your voice, and your image. If you look in front of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I ask that Exhibit P416 be placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at that piece of paper, does that contain your name and date of birth at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. The witness, could you please just move forward to the table, approach the microphone as closely as possible. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are two other names that appear on that paper with two numbers alongside of them. If you would like to use those names in the testimony, can you please not use the name but just the numbers that are next to them. Don't refer to the people's names. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in April 1992 where did you live?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live in the town of Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you live in an apartment or a house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: A house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long had you lived in Foca in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Fifty years. Fifty years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far did you live from the centre, the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Near the centre.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Smith. Could you switch off the microphone while the witness is answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you married at the time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they living away from home at the time or with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: They did not live with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you working at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you define yourself ethnically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Bosniak, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 were you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you serving in any military unit?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war started in 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in your house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, can you tell the Court what you saw when the war started on that first day.

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Yes. Gunfire started. From all sides fire was opened on Foca. That is what I saw and heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in your house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: I stayed in the house five days, five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the fifth day did you decide to leave your house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you decide to leave?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Well, because I was afraid they might kill me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: The Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you think the Chetniks may kill you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Well, because they were killing all the Muslims, so I guess they would have -- they were very likely to kill me too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say Chetniks, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Serb troops who had come from Serbia and Montenegro. They were all Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that they were killing Muslims. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: They were killing both Muslims and Croats. I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any killing of Muslims or Croats whilst you were in your house for that five days, or is it what you heard through other people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: I heard it from other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you decide to go on that fifth day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: I decided to head for Gorazde, to leave Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you leave in your car?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was with you? Don't state their names, just their relationships.

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: My son and my wife. My son and wife were with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to Gorazde, or did you stop somewhere along the way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: I stopped at Ustikolina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you stop there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Because there were some troops there. There was the Yugoslav army there and soldiers, and I thought that they were there and that they would protect us, that we were safe there, that we would be sheltered there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the commander of those troops, does his name appear on that page in front of you? But don't state the name if it does.

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What number appears alongside his name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were some troops at this location. Was there also a military warehouse?

utterances.speaker: FWS-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this military warehouse?
